prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, in which magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms made accuracy and stability at the 10^-18 level possible.

statement.case_for: I keep optical lattice clocks, with Katori and Ye, as my final single-part position, and after the full exchange I hold it more firmly on its science than I did after the openings. The physics is a single, bounded mechanism: the magic-wavelength condition cancels the lattice light shift, Lamb-Dicke confinement removes Doppler and recoil effects, and many neutral atoms are interrogated at once on an ultranarrow optical transition, so that stability and accuracy improve together. The consequences are demonstrated and not only promised: fractional uncertainties near 1e-18 reproduced with Sr, Yb and Hg in several laboratories, international comparisons, and use in tests of fundamental constants and relativistic geodesy. On the chair's question about novelty, the distinction I would put in the record is functional. A frequency comb counts optical cycles, and an ion clock controls one quantum system; the lattice clock is the ensemble solution that removed the trade-off between confinement and a perturbation-free transition, and it exposed the many-body, collisional and blackbody physics that now sets the limit. On credit, I accept the division the other members describe, Katori for the concept and first realisation and Ye for taking performance to the frontier, but I want to be clear that I treat it as recollection and not as something the supplied record documents. I therefore support a citation that names the invention and its realisation and the mechanism, and that does not rest on a single record number or claim to settle priority among lattice-clock laboratories. I agree with Mehlig and Eriksson that the redefinition of the second is a question of timing and not of scientific doubt, and the consistent support across members from different fields is a reason to scrutinise the case, which I have done, and not a reason to accept it.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is unchanged: a committee could still read lattice clocks as an outstanding refinement of precision spectroscopy already honoured in 2005 and 2012, and I cannot dispel that reading with evidence from the supplied record, only with the physical argument above. A second reservation is that the two-name credit leaves out other lattice-clock groups and the ion-clock line, so the prize would be a defensible simplification and not the only possible allocation; Kroll's mention of Takamoto and Pearce's list of NIST, PTB, SYRTE and JILA colleagues make this a real cost. Third, the formal redefinition of the second has not happened, so part of the impact is still prospective. Finally, a precision-metrology capability is a different kind of result from a discovery about nature or a new quantum phenomenon, and if the committee decides that this year should recognise the latter, B057 is the stronger answer, provided the credit problem of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang can be solved honestly.

responses.point: Kroll describes the credit as fitting two names cleanly, with Katori for the concept and early strontium realisation and Ye for taking performance to the frontier, while listing Takamoto, SYRTE, PTB and NIST/JILA beyond Ye as contributors outside the credit.
responses.response: I take this as an answer to the chair's attribution question only in part. Kroll's own list of contributors outside the credit shows that the two-name boundary is a judgment, not a verified fact, and I do not think we can settle it from the supplied record. What I can say is that the physical roles are distinct and both necessary: the magic-wavelength proposal and first realisation, and the systematic control that turned it into a 10^-18 clock. That is why I keep both names, and why I would word the citation around the invention and its realisation so that it does not adjudicate between the many groups that later matured the technology.

responses.point: Lindroth argues from atomic structure that controlling blackbody, higher-order light-shift and collisional systematics is a substantial achievement and not only engineering, and she asks whether lattice and ion clocks should be recognised jointly.
responses.response: Her point about the systematics is the best answer I have seen to the objection that this is an instrument advance, and as a theorist working with qubit coherence I recognise the difficulty of pushing an error budget to this level. On the joint recognition question I still resist, now more firmly. Single-ion control was recognised in 2012, and bringing an ion-clock laureate into B012 would exceed the three-person limit or force a choice between ion-clock groups for which the supplied material gives no basis. A bounded lattice-clock citation is the more honest one.

responses.point: Danielsson keeps B039 as his main fallback, calls the Higgs observation the most consequential experimental result on the shortlist, and asks whether the pending redefinition of the second is a precondition for recognition or a confirmation of impact.
responses.response: I agree that B039 is consequential and I do not think its weaker position reflects a weaker science case; the difficulty is that the four-person credit cannot be reduced to three without a rule about leadership versus authorship that we have not agreed on. On his question, I treat the redefinition as a confirmation and not a precondition: the clocks already operate at 10^-18 and are used in comparisons and tests, and a prize that waited for a metrological body's decision would make our judgment depend on an external schedule. My earlier question for him, what would move B012 higher, is answered by his own move in round 1, and I see no remaining disagreement between us on the preferred configuration.

responses.point: Eriksson says his weighting of electronic-structure stories was too parochial, that B012 has the cleanest attribution on the list, and that the metrology-versus-discovery objection is inadequate given the history of precision-measurement prizes.
responses.response: I agree with the last point and would add the practical form of it: the prize has repeatedly gone to measurements that changed what can be done, and the question for B012 is whether it did. I am less comfortable with calling the attribution the cleanest on the list, since every member who supports B012 also lists omitted groups. It is cleaner than the three- and four-name collaboration cases, but not clean in an absolute sense. On B051, I accept his reservation about a second superconducting-circuit prize so soon after 2025 and it reinforces my decision to keep that item only as a disclosed alternative.

responses.point: Olsson asks how much weight prospective impacts such as the redefinition of the second and clock-based geodesy should carry against demonstrated results, and notes that the credit boundary is defensible but not unique.
responses.response: I would count demonstrated results first: reproduction with three species at 10^-18, international comparisons and measurements of the gravitational redshift over small height differences are already in the record, and those are enough for maturity. Searches for varying constants and geodesy at scale are prospective and I would not cite them as the basis of the prize. I think this answers her concern in practice, because the case does not need a redefinition or a detection of new physics, and I would keep both out of the citation.

responses.point: Pearce, who moved from IceCube to B012, grants the argument that IceCube or the Higgs carry more weight with the wider community than a precision-metrology result, and asks whether other groups such as NIST, PTB and SYRTE make a two-name credit a simplification.
responses.response: I accept that a discovery prize in particle or astroparticle physics would be better known, but wider recognition is not part of the statutory test. The question is whether the committee can write a defensible citation, and for B012 it can, while for B029 and B039 several members, Pearce included, doubt that the allocation among Halzen, Karle, Spiering and the AMANDA and Baikal pioneers, or among the four Higgs names, can be made fairly. On the two-name simplification we agree, and I would put it in the citation's wording and not hide it.

uncertainties: Whether the committee treats lattice clocks as a distinct invention beyond the 2005 and 2012 prizes; I have argued it on physics but the judgment is partly about taste in how much novelty is enough.
The priority and relative roles of Katori, Ye and other groups, which no member can verify from the supplied record and which I take from general knowledge.
Whether B057 would become the better answer if the committee prefers a new quantum phenomenon, and whether its credit can be fixed within three names.
Whether the committee will want formal recusal ruling on B051 if it is advanced.
statement.conflict_note: My disclosure is unchanged. I have a specific connection to B051: my own research is in circuit and waveguide QED, I direct the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology, and Chalmers colleagues Per Delsing and C. M. Wilson and my frequent co-author Anton Frisk Kockum work in this area; Chalmers also hosted researchers associated with the 2025 prize. I would not advocate B051 and would ask for a recusal ruling if it were advanced, which answers the chair's fifth question as far as I am concerned. I have no specific personal or institutional conflict with Katori, Ye or B012, and none apparent for B057.
